title: The transformer block - attention, MLP, residual and layer norm

questions.prompt: What are the four parts of a transformer block, in the order the operations happen in a pre-norm block?
options: attention -> MLP -> residual -> layer norm
layer norm -> attention -> residual -> layer norm -> MLP -> residual
MLP -> attention -> residual -> layer norm -> residual
embedding -> attention -> softmax -> output
questions.explain: In a pre-norm block: normalise, run attention, add the input back (residual); normalise again, run the MLP, add the input back (residual). The tempting wrong answer is the first one, which is a plausible-sounding order that puts the residual in the wrong place and layer norm at the end - post-norm ordering, which was the original 2017 form but is now the less common choice because it trains worse.

questions.prompt: Why does a transformer block need an MLP at all? Attention alone cannot do the job, because...
options: The MLP is what converts the final vector into output logits
Attention output is a weighted average of values that already exist, so it can move information around but cannot compute a new feature; the MLP is where the actual thinking happens
Attention output vectors are not normalised, so the MLP normalises them
The MLP supplies the query and key vectors that attention needs
questions.explain: Attention mixes what is already there. The MLP applies a small nonlinear function independently at every position, and that is where new features are computed. The tempting wrong answer is the first one - the logits come from a separate output projection after the final block, not from the MLP inside each block.

questions.prompt: What is the gradient-level reason the residual connection helps a 100-block stack train at all?
options: It gives the gradient a direct, unobstructed path back to earlier layers instead of forcing it through 100 nonlinearities
It removes the need for layer norm
It makes the attention weights sum to 1
It reduces the number of parameters in the block
questions.explain: Adding the input back means the gradient can flow back along a straight highway instead of being multiplied by 100 Jacobians, which is exactly the vanishing-gradient problem examples/03_train_linear.py names: 'why deep networks need tricks (residual connections, careful initialisation, normalisation)'. The tempting wrong answer is the second one - layer norm is still needed; the residual connection and the norm solve different problems.

questions.prompt: What does layer norm do to a vector, and what does it deliberately leave alone?
options: It clips every component into [0, 1], discarding anything outside that range
It sorts the components so the largest is first
It rescales the vector to have mean about 0 and standard deviation about 1, deliberately keeping the direction - the information - while taming the magnitude
It converts the vector into a probability distribution that sums to 1
questions.explain: Layer norm subtracts the mean, divides by the standard deviation, then applies a learned scale and shift. The direction of the vector carries the information; the magnitude is what drifts as you stack blocks, and a drifted magnitude pushes the next softmax into the saturated zone L22 warned about. The tempting wrong answer is the last one - that is what softmax does, and softmax is a different operation on a different axis.

questions.prompt: In this repo, which part of the harness actually sees any of the block's internals?
options: The metrics inspect the attention weights to compute ECE
The harness re-implements the block to check the vendor's numbers
The provider adapters log the layer-norm outputs
None of it - the harness is deliberately blind to the mechanism and measures only the returned probabilities, accuracy, calibration and swap safety
questions.explain: decisionarena/providers.py sends the raw state string to a vendor and decisionarena/metrics.py measures what comes back. That separation - mechanism versus measurement - is the architecture of the project, as examples/04_attention_numpy.py's closing block states: 'The harness does not care HOW the model does that.' The tempting wrong answer is the second one: the harness never re-implements a model, because the point is to measure the model as a black box.
